items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Next door would be the Three Deuces, John Kirby.

ctx.x: Yeah, he was fortunate. But that’s when places like Birdland opened up. Of course, Kelly’s Stable on 52nd Street, they had live music in there. They had Nat King Cole trio, Coleman Hawkins, Teddy Wilson, they had everybody. And Ben Webster, Don Byas, they were

all playing in there at one time. Then you’d go down the street to the Hickory House, there would be Billy Taylor and his trio, Buddy Rich would be playing with Joe Marsala, I think that was the band he played with. End of CD #3 Then you go to the Famous Door, there would be the Count Basie band. Across the street there would be Ryan’s, Jimmy Ryan’s. There would be Wilbur de Paris, brothers, they would have a band over there. Next door would be the Three Deuces, John Kirby. Oh, it was so much music in New York in…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Because like John Kirby, started the little band playing in the little clubs, you know.

ctx.x: Because here you'd spent 15 years in big bands. Now here, you'd stayed with Basie and big bands had collapsed.

That's right. That's right. And the one that I really was dependent on, you know. I thought Basie would go on forever, which he will, but there was a lapse in that time, you know. He was broke from the big band. He'd spent a lot of money trying to keep it together. And it just got -- there was no place for a big band to work, see. Because like John Kirby, started the little band playing in the little clubs, you know. And the dance halls were collapsing. The big bands were collapsing, there was no big bands to…
No. Duke could supplement his thing because --
